title: Why You Should Observe Your Students More https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/12/15/why-you-should-observe-your-students-more/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin challenges the assumption that constant hands-on helping equals good teaching, arguing that most teachers don't observe their students enough. He explains that hovering and reteaching after every lesson is actually associated with ineffective classroom management, academic immaturity, and chaos. Quiet, focused observation during independent work instead reduces misbehavior, builds tenacious independence, boosts accomplishment, and gives teachers deeper insight into each student's needs. He describes what real observation looks like: standing, undivided attention across the whole room, paired with sharp lessons and thorough checks for understanding beforehand. The piece closes with an image of a fully engaged, independently working class as the true mark of good teaching.
points: Excessive hands-on helping after lessons is linked to poor classroom management and academic immaturity, not good teaching.
Quiet, standing observation during independent work reduces misbehavior because most misbehavior happens when a teacher's back is turned or attention is elsewhere.
Stepping back from constant helping builds tenaciously independent students who ask smarter questions and need less assistance.
Observation deepens a teacher's knowledge of students, sharpening lesson planning and pacing.
True observation requires vibrant lessons and a solid check for understanding beforehand so students are ready to work alone.
quotes: But the truth is, going overboard in helping students doesn’t make you a good teacher. In fact, it’s a sign of trouble.
Most misbehavior happens when your back is turned, when you’re talking, or when you’re otherwise busy and distracted with other things.
If you’re in the habit of helping students immediately following lessons, then you’re training them to be dependant on you.
Immediate, focused, and independent practice of whatever you teach your students is critical to their success and associated with better learning and faster progress.
Observation entails an undivided focus on your students—always standing and typically at a distance that allows you to watch your entire class.
Independent work means not dependent on you. And frequent periods of it—silent, focused, and uninterrupted—isn’t too much to ask of any group of students.
